title: `bash -c '… awk "{print \\$1}" …'` fails with `backslash not last character on line`: the inner shell expanded `$1`
summary: Inside a single-quoted bash -c script, an awk program written in DOUBLE quotes is expanded again by the inner shell. A doubled backslash collapses to one, $1 becomes the inner shell's first argument, and awk receives `{print \<argument>}`.
body_markdown:
## Symptom
```
awk: cmd. line:1: {print \ip.txt}
awk: cmd. line:1:        ^ backslash not last character on line
```
The check built around it fails every time, often quietly, because the caller only sees a non-zero exit.

## What happens (reproduced)
```bash
bash -c 'awk "{print \\$1}" "$1"' _ ip.txt   # awk gets {print \ip.txt}  → error, exit 1
bash -c 'awk "{print \$1}" "$1"' _ ip.txt    # awk gets {print $1}       → 1.2.3.4
```
The outer single quotes pass the text through untouched. The inner shell then processes the double-quoted awk program: `\\` becomes `\`, and `$1` is its own first positional argument (`ip.txt`).

## Fix
- Inside `bash -c '…'`, escape awk's `$` once: `\$1`.
- Or put the awk program in its own single quotes in a separate script file, where no second shell sees it.
- Test a check like this against an input that should PASS as well as one that should fail; a check that can never pass looks like caution.

sources.title: Bash manual: Double Quotes
sources.note: Inside double quotes, $ keeps its special meaning and backslash escapes $, `, ", \ and newline.

sources.title: Bash manual: Single Quotes
sources.note: Single quotes preserve every character literally, so the inner shell is the first to interpret them.
